name: Money Laundering Networks
title: Money Laundering Networks
answer: Money laundering networks are the connected sets of people, accounts, companies, and payment channels used to move and disguise the origin of criminal proceeds. In fraud detection and forensics, the scope covers the layering and integration stages, from smurfing and mule accounts to shell company chains, trade based laundering, and crypto mixing. The work sits inside The AI Accountant because the same ledger, entity resolution, and anomaly detection methods used in audit and fraud review apply to network tracing. Analysts look for patterns of shared devices, addresses, beneficial owners, and transaction timing that reveal a network rather than isolated bad actors.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Money laundering networks are the connected sets of people, accounts, companies, and payment channels used to move and disguise the origin of criminal proceeds. In fraud detection and forensics, the scope covers the layering and integration stages, from smurfing and mule accounts to shell company chains, trade based laundering, and crypto mixing. The work sits inside The AI Accountant because the same ledger, entity resolution, and anomaly detection methods used in audit and fraud review apply to network tracing. Analysts look for patterns of shared devices, addresses, beneficial owners, and transaction timing that reveal a network rather than isolated bad actors.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for tracing money laundering networks draws on transaction ledgers from banks and payment providers, customer due diligence records, corporate registry filings, sanctions and politically exposed person lists, and public crypto ledgers. These feeds land in data warehouses and graph databases, where entity resolution links names, addresses, phone numbers, and account identifiers that may appear in different formats. Analysts use link analysis and graph queries to follow funds through mule accounts, shell companies, and exchange deposits. Case management systems hold the resulting alerts, evidence, and audit trails.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with data preparation, where transaction records, identity records, and external lists are cleaned and matched into a single entity graph. Analysts then apply rule based typologies, such as structuring below reporting thresholds or rapid pass through of funds, alongside statistical and machine learning models that score nodes and edges for suspicion. Graph algorithms find communities, central actors, and shortest paths between known bad actors and new accounts. Investigators review the highest risk clusters, gather supporting documents, and decide whether to close, monitor, or escalate the case.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Money laundering detection sits under anti money laundering and counter terrorist financing rules, which impose customer due diligence, record keeping, and suspicious activity reporting duties. The data used is sensitive, so access controls, purpose limitation, and retention schedules matter, and cross border sharing can be restricted by local law. Models that flag networks can produce false positives that harm innocent customers, so institutions need documented validation, explainability, and human review before any account is closed or report is filed. Provenance of both the underlying records and the model outputs must be preserved so that a decision can be reconstructed later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real time monitoring as instant payment rails and crypto transfers reduce the window for after the fact review. Detection is converging with fraud analytics, because the same networks often run scams, mule recruitment, and laundering through the same accounts. Privacy enhancing techniques and federated learning are being explored to share risk signals across institutions without pooling raw customer data. Regulators and standard setters continue to push for more consistent beneficial ownership registries and clearer expectations for AI used in compliance.
